1.note: Microfilm history of the room is irrelevant to the lending program; B and C misstate what the sentence does.

2.note: Comma splice; a colon introduces the evidence of popularity. B is a run-on, D is wordy and nonstandard.

3.note: Parallel with 'to own' and uses 'than' for comparison; C breaks parallelism, B is the wrong word.

4.note: Singular subject 'A family' takes 'saves'; the relative clause is a distractor.

5.note: 'Looks like a bargain' requires a small budget; the other three are synonyms of extravagant (one-of-four-differs).

6.note: Semicolon joins two independent clauses; B is a comma splice, C a run-on, D has a misplaced comma.

7.note: The preceding contrast (books cheap, ladders not) makes ladder lending follow from the original purpose, so 'Thus' is right; 'Nevertheless' wrongly signals contrast.

8.note: Records indicate a conclusion; 'insinuate', 'proclaim' and 'allege' carry the wrong connotation.

10.note: Only C names an outcome the funding would bring about; A, B and D name actions or history rather than a result. This option is the original text.

11.note: Paired commas set off the parenthetical 'or as successfully'; C leaves the second comma out.

12.note: 'These trips' needs the preceding sentence about the father taking the children along, so the addition goes at point C, before his death.

13.note: A plural family name used as a subject takes no apostrophe.

14.note: An appositive noun phrase follows an independent clause, so a colon is right; a semicolon or a period leaves a fragment, and no punctuation is a fused construction.

16.note: Plural 'stones' and past narration require 'contained'; A and C are singular.

17.note: She was never a member and could not attend, so 'barred' fits; banished, exiled and evicted imply prior membership.

18.note: A comma before the coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses; no comma after 'but'.

19.note: The addition supports 'Recognition came slowly' and contrasts with the final sentence about labels carrying her name; A misreads paragraph 4.

20.note: Discoveries paired with exclusion from the Society match 'without formal standing'; C is the only option aligned with the stated purpose.

21.note: The next sentences explain weaving versus embroidery, which the not-a-tapestry claim sets up; the others are off topic.

22.note: Comma splice; a colon introduces the explanation. C misuses '; but', and D fuses the clauses.

23.note: Plural 'captions' takes 'name'; present tense matches the paragraph.

25.note: A victory celebration stitched by the defeated is unusual; A, B and D all mean ordinary or minor (one-of-four-differs).

26.note: Neutral 'crowded'; the other three carry negative pest or disease connotations (one-of-four-differs).

27.note: The ships and chain mail are examples of the 'detail' named in the preceding sentence.

28.note: Comma splice fixed with a period; C is still a splice, and D changes the meaning (an omen, which it is).

29.note: The sentence offers a possible ending after 'no one knows how the story originally ended'; it does not explain why the section is missing.

30.note: Standard series commas, plus a comma after the introductory phrase.

31.note: The sun stands 'highest'; loftiest, tallest and steepest are imprecise.

32.note: The sentence explains why 'this hardly mattered', so 'After all' fits; it is not a contrast or a result.

33.note: 'Each railroad' takes the singular possessive 'its', matching 'its headquarters' later in the sentence.

34.note: The sentence gives a concrete picture of the confusion; it does not repeat the train sentence, and paragraph 1 has no station clocks.

35.note: Singular 'risk' needs a singular verb; past 'grew' parallels 'missed'. C and D are plural forms.

36.note: Correlative 'not from X but from Y' is parallel; D drops the second 'from' (non-parallel), B mismatches neither/but, and C uses 'and'.

37.note: No punctuation between subject and verb.

38.note: Detroit illustrates 'kept their old clocks for years'; 1905 is still within a generation, so A fails.

39.note: Past perfect fits the past narration and the later 'forgot'.

40.note: Comma splice fixed with a relative clause 'by which time'; B adds a stray 'and', and C fuses the clauses.
